episodes.title: GPs, LPs, and the anatomy of a PE fund
takeaways: A PE fund is typically a limited partnership: LPs supply capital passively and are liable only up to their commitment, while the GP makes the decisions and carries legal responsibility.
Capital is committed up front but called only as needed, and the closed-end fund runs about ten years, so your sponsor's behavior is shaped by where the fund sits in its life.
Your sponsor answers to LPs and reports valuations to them, and lenders lend to your company, not the fund, so understanding the fund helps you read board, lender, and capital-allocation decisions.

episodes.title: Fund economics: management fees, hurdle rates, carry, and the waterfall
takeaways: The management fee, often about two percent, pays the GP firm to operate and is usually charged on committed capital early on; the real upside is carry, typically twenty percent of profit, paid only after LPs clear a hurdle, often eight percent compounded.

In a waterfall, cash flows in order: return of capital, preferred return, GP catch-up, then an eighty-twenty split; whole-fund and deal-by-deal versions change when the GP gets paid and how much risk it has an incentive to take.

For an operating executive, carry is earned at exit, so timing, EBITDA quality, and clean numbers matter. Sponsor fees paid by your company are watched and capped by lenders, and the sponsor reads your results against the whole fund.

episodes.title: The fund lifecycle and why the clock drives every decision
takeaways: A PE fund runs about ten years: roughly five years of investing, then a harvest period focused on exits, with possible extensions. Fees step down as it ages, so carry and realized cash matter more.

Time changes returns: the same 2.5 times money multiple is about a 20 percent IRR over five years but only about 14 percent over seven, and LPs judge the GP by cash returned (DPI) when it raises the next fund.

Know where your sponsor's fund is in its life, present initiatives with a timing case that shows payback before the likely exit window, and start legal, compliance, and retention readiness well before a sale.
